svg.title: WHERE CAN A PARK-OUT BUS CHARGE?
svg.desc: A park-out school bus needs about 133 kWh a day, about 267 kWh in deep winter, and has a 194 kWh battery. Five options are tested: a 100 A home with electric heat gives about 86 kWh, short; a 100 A home with load management fills the 194 kWh battery, covering the need just; a shared hub for 20 buses on about 220 kW covers it; in deep winter a 25 kW mid-day charge at school adds about 100 kWh, covering the winter need; driveway delivery works but costs about 11,000 dollars a bus a year, the weakest option.

g.text: WHERE CAN A PARK-OUT BUS CHARGE?
A bus that sleeps at the driver’s home needs about 133 kWh a day (80 miles), about 267 kWh in deep winter.

svg.text: One Type C electric bus · 194 kWh battery

g.text: About 7 kW to spare overnight after the house’s own load:
DRIVER’S HOME · 100 A, WITH LOAD MANAGEMENT
About 16 kW to spare on a typical night: fills the
194 kWh battery, only if a device holds the bus back.
SHARED HUB AT A SCHOOL OR MUNICIPAL LOT
20 buses × 133 kWh ≈ 220 kW average overnight. A lot with
about 250 kW spare manages it with charging control.
DEEP WINTER · ADD A MID-DAY CHARGE AT SCHOOL
Need rises to about 267 kWh, above the 194 kWh battery. After a
full overnight charge, 25 kW for 4 hours at school adds about 100 kWh.
Energy is possible to deliver, but at the AXIVAI stress-test
rate it costs about $11,000 a bus a year.
Verdicts on each card. AXIVAI estimates.
do the work. Driveway delivery is weakest.
Outside New York City, 96% of the state’s school buses return to a depot overnight:
Home figures assume 240 V service, household plus bus kept to 80% of the rating, a 12-hour window. Not measured at real homes.
AXIVAI estimates; PowerUp NYC; NY State roadmap; DOE Electric School Bus guide; WRI.
